proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘Worrying about Emotions in History’ (2002) Rosenwein argues that Peter and Carol Stearns's emotionology (1985) confines emotional standards to the modern age of middle-class advice manuals and, ‘tapping Huizinga’, dismisses the premodern period as having ‘less precise’ standards.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own text. Printed pp. 824–826 were read in the atlas's earlier recorded reading (see the 2026-10-28 addendum to dc166_rosenwein_worrying_2002); on 2026-10-31 the same Stearns section and notes 9–22 were reread in the unlicensed repost transcription already named in that addendum (no printed page numbers in that text, so the 824–826 locators rest on the earlier reading). She introduces ‘Peter Stearns and his psychiatrist/historian wife Carol Stearns’ and their ‘emotionology’ (n. 9: AHR 90, 1985, 813–36; n. 12 quotes their definition); ‘But it turned out to be a very shallow past’; ‘The Stearnses’ answer: by looking at popular advice manuals’; ‘Tapping Huizinga (with grateful acknowledgment), the Stearnses claim that the pre-modern period had “less precise” standards’ (n. 18: Anger, 21–23, 25); ‘This broad dismissal of the period’; on her reading emotionology ‘by definition belongs to the modern period’. The concept is jointly credited to Carol Z. Stearns, who is not an atlas endpoint; the edge attaches to Peter N. Stearns as co-author. Her criticism is her argument, not an adjudication; Stearns's 2010 answers (Plamper interview, pp. 261–265, recorded on the atlas source) are not treated as a reply to her. This lifts the hold recorded in the entry scope note now that 824–826 are read. Distinct from edge_2320 (Elias → Stearns) and edge_2321 (Stearns → Delumeau).

review.reason: Held on provenance only. The quoted phrases exist verbatim in the unlicensed repost text (re-fetched: 'psychiatrist/historian wife Carol Stearns', 'But it turned out to be a very shallow past', 'by looking at popular advice manuals', 'Tapping Huizinga (with grateful acknowledgment)', '“less precise” standards', 'This broad dismissal', 'emotionology by definition belongs to the modern period'), and the critique is fairly worded. But neither reading route is acceptable: (1) the printed pp. 824–826 locators rest on the 2026-10-28 reading of an unauthorised course copy, which the user's provenance rule excludes (course scans); (2) the the site used is not a licensed host; the domain now hosts a commercial popular-history site (mythology and timeline listicles, ) that reposts the AHR article under 'Journal' with no AHR/OUP attribution, publication data or licence statement. It is functionally an unlicensed mirror and should be treated as unread. To lift: read pp. 824–826 in an authorised copy (OUP or JSTOR stable 10.1086/532498 through library access) and re-cite with printed pages. No content doubt.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rosenwein (2002) places Delumeau's Sin and Fear within the narrative of medieval emotional excess and asks whether he is ‘right to jump from scary sources to real fear’, calling instead for attention to reception and local contexts of meaning.
proposed_edges.map_label: From scary sources to real fear?, 2002
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own text, read 2026-10-31 in the unlicensed repost transcription (section on Delumeau and Peter Dinzelbacher; printed pages not visible there and not collated with the published pagination). The paragraph beginning ‘Jean Delumeau adds fear to the heady brew’ (notes 49–50, citing Sin and Fear, 21 and 240, i.e. the 1990 English translation) sets him within the grand narrative; the paragraph beginning ‘The strength of both Delumeau and Dinzelbacher’ (notes 54–56) asks ‘But are they right to jump from scary sources to real fear?’ and answers with varied responses to frightening images and a call for reception theory and ‘local contexts of meaning’. Earlier, in her account of Stearns's review, she concedes ‘There is plenty to criticize about Delumeau’s approach’ (note 17). Delumeau's books (1983 French original; 1990 translation) are unread. Her critique is shared with Dinzelbacher, who is not an atlas endpoint. Distinct from edge_2321 (Stearns's critique of Delumeau as quoted by Rosenwein).

review.reason: Held on provenance only, as bhr_rel_01. Quotes verified verbatim in the unlicensed repost text ('Jean Delumeau adds fear to the heady brew', 'But are they right to jump from scary sources to real fear?', 'local contexts of meaning', 'There is plenty to criticize about Delumeau’s approach'), but that route is not acceptable (see bhr_rel_01 and provenance_flags), and the Delumeau/Dinzelbacher pages were never read in printed form, so the edge has no authorised reading and no printed locator. To lift: read the Delumeau/Dinzelbacher section (notes 49–56) in OUP/JSTOR and give printed pages. Note also that Rosenwein's line 'Delumeau and Dinzelbacher teach us pointedly that historians of emotion need to attend to reception theory' is ironic; the wording 'calling instead for attention to reception' is a fair paraphrase.
